title: Individual differences in sharing false political information on social media: Direct and indirect effects of cognitive-perceptual schizotypy and psychopathy
screen_reason: Two preregistered online surveys of US adults (Prolific) report the share of respondents answering 'yes' to having ever shared a political news story that was made up — both inadvertently ('later found out was made up') and deliberately ('thought AT THE TIME was made up'). These are self-reported SHARING shares with explicit denominators (Table 1), i.e. RECALL/sharing estimates, even though the paper's aim is individual differences.

estimates.country: US (US citizens, resident in the US)
estimates.platform: Social media (general; Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, Instagram, Discord, Reddit named as examples)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who have ever shared a political news story online that they later found out was made up (Study 1)
estimates.denominator: 507 US adult social media users drawn from the Prolific research panel (Study 1, after data screening from 550 recorded responses)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'yes' to 'Have you ever shared a political news story online that you later found out was made up?' (lifetime, inadvertent sharing)
estimates.misinfo_def: ‘Misinformation’ refers to false material that people spread in the mistaken belief that it is true.
estimates.source_quote: Have you ever shared a political news story online that you later found out was made up? No 404 (79.7%) 424 (80.5%) Yes 103 (20.3%) 103 (19.5%)
estimates.page_loc: Table 1 (Demographic data: Study 1 and 2), p. 4; Study 1 column
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own retrospective judgement; two binary yes/no items adapted from Barthel et al. (2016) and Buchanan (2020). No external verification of the stories; authors flag recall and social-desirability bias as limitations.
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were drawn from the Prolific research panel, and paid £1 GBP each. Inclusion criteria were that the participants be US citizens, resident in the US, who had English as a first language, had not participated in any previous related studies, and had indicated they were not members of any other crowdsourced research panels
estimates.notes: Data-collection date not stated anywhere in the paper; year set to publication year 2021 (received 13 April 2021). Non-probability opt-in panel (Prolific), quota-style recruitment in two age waves (18-40, over 40). Study 1 and Study 2 are independent samples of the same population using identical items; if only one row per cell can be pooled, Study 1 (N = 507) is the larger-context primary. missed_or_uncertain: (1) Pooled cross-tabulation of both studies (N = 1034) gives verbatim mutually exclusive shares: '138 (13.3%) participants said they had only shared a political story they later found out was untrue; 59 (5.7%) said they had only shared one they knew at the time was untrue; 68 (6.6%) had done both; and 769 (74.4%) had done neither.' These are a decomposition of the same two items already extracted; adding them would double-count, so no rows were created. The Discussion's 'around a quarter of individuals report sharing false political information' is a complement of 74.4% computed by the authors and is not extracted per R8. (2) Group sizes in the t-tests (e.g. 'the 284 who had not (M = 1.84, SD = 1.17) and the 69 who had') are restricted to the CRT-2 subsample (n = 353) and are not population estimates. (3) 'Shares political info' means (Study 1 M = 2.13 on 1-5) are scale means about political information in general, not misinformation, and are not shares. (4) Subgroup breakdowns by gender/education exist only as regression coefficients, not as shares.

rob.design: Two preregistered cross-sectional online questionnaires (Qualtrics) with non-probability panel samples of US adults from Prolific: Study 1 N = 507 retained from 550 recorded, Study 2 N = 527 from 551; recruitment in two age waves (18-40, over 40); no response rate reported (panel opt-in); exclusions for straightlining, non-use of social media, implausible demographics and suspected duplicate responding; exposure/sharing measured with two single binary self-report items (no reliability statistic possible); trait scales reported Cronbach's alpha 0.78-0.93 except CRT-2 alpha = 0.52.
rob.item6_quote: These were “Have you ever shared a political news story online that you later found out was made up?”, then “And have you ever shared a political news story online that you thought AT THE TIME was made up?”. Both were answered by selecting ‘yes’ or ‘no’.
